catalog_quote: Stress is by far the most complex component of Manam phonology. Even though, with a few exceptions, Manam stress is predictable, its assignment is governed by a large number of rules, some of which have phonological conditioning, others are conditioned morphologically. ... There is one general condition on primary stress position in Manam: no primary stress can be farther from the end of a word than its antepenultimate syllable. If no other factors intervene, Manam primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable: ... pátu 'stone' ... tanépwa 'chief' ... If, however, the second vowel from the end of a word is immediately preceded by another vowel, the stress is antepenultimate, provided no morpheme boundary intervenes between the antepenultimate vowel and the end of the word. ... móasi 'song' góai 'star' ... sweep_summary: Manam (mana1295) is in the catalog as 'weight' on Lichtenberk 1983 (A grammar of Manam, sect. 2.7, pp. 50-56). this search of works with stress in the title turned up exactly one stress-titled bibliography item, Chaski, 'Linear and Metrical Analyses of Manam Stress', Oceanic Linguistics 25(1/2): 167-209, DOI 10.2307/3623211 (Glottolog dates it 1985, the DOI record 1986). It is squarely about Manam word stress but is closed everywhere checked (JSTOR bot-challenge/paywall, Semantic Scholar CLOSED, OpenAlex closed with no repository fulltext, no archive.org copy; the Crossref and OpenAlex records and the JSTOR landing page were and logged in there. Second-hand, the held Buckley 1994/1997 papers describe it as an earlier metrical treatment whose data are Lichtenberk's, so it is a reanalysis and unlikely to change the classification; priority medium (it is the only dedicated article and StressTyp2 cites it, and it could settle the record's 'contra' note on StressTyp2's superheavy/heavy chain). No new first-hand statement was obtained; the on-disk Turner 1986 SIL teaching grammar (sect. 2.4, pp. 22-24) and Lichtenberk 1983 sect. 2.7 were re-read and both confirm the catalog's classification (three-syllable window, penult default, closed nasal-final syllables attract stress, suffix-conditioned antepenult, a few lexical exceptions). catalog's classification stands; deciding source not superseded.

new_statements.quote: The stressed syllable in Manam is either the last syllable of a word, or the next-to-last, or the syllable before the next-to-last. In other words, the stressed syllable has to be one of the last three syllables of the word. The stress usually falls on the next-to-last syllable. [p. 22] ... Now if the word ends in a consonant, then the last syllable is stressed. [p. 23: gabagabam 'your elbow', natum 'your child', bureng 'coconut oil'] ... Several suffixes (but not all of them), when they come at the end of a word, require that the stress fall on the syllable before the next-to-last. If the next-to-last syllable, however, ends in a consonant, then it will be stressed instead. [p. 24] ... Stress on a few words in Manam is unpredictable [p. 24]

new_statements.reading: Three-syllable right window, default penult, consonant-final (nasal-coda) syllable attracts stress, certain suffixes push stress to the antepenult unless the penult is closed, a few lexical exceptions -- an independent fieldworker's account that matches the catalog's 'weight' coding and Lichtenberk 1983's Rules 17/19 point for point. Lichtenberk 1983 sect. 2.7 (the catalog's deciding source, held by the project at lines 7878-8115) was also re-opened in this search of works with stress in the title and the deciding quotation verified verbatim ('no primary stress can be farther from the end of a word than its antepenultimate syllable'; 'If no other factors intervene, Manam primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable' Rule 19; 'Words that contain closed syllables are stressed on those syllables, unless the closed syllable is antepenultimate, and a morpheme boundary intervenes between it and the end of the word, or the word is an intransitive verb' Rule 17). Nothing read this search of works with stress in the title is more authoritative than Lichtenberk.

sources.quote: 'Manam has phonemic stress functioning on a grammatical level: 'godoki 'take it' / go'doki 'take them'; 'gokang 'eat it' / go'kang 'eat them''. Syllable patterns list closed types VC, CVC, CVVC, CVVVC ('Only the nasals /m/ and /ng/ occur word finally'); 'Phonemic stress if written, is indicated by underlining the vowel in the stressed syllable.' Nothing on closed-syllable attraction or the default position.
